tier_reason: docs/SIMD_BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md carries the v1.5.x primitive table (AVX2+FMA 3.4x/1.7x/2.5x/4.9x, NEON 2.1x/1.8x/8.0x/3.0x, AVX-512 5.0x/3.9x/1.3x/8.5x) and the NEON exp 2.1x to 2.5-2.6x row from tools/simd_verification (Release, Mac Mini M1); the benchmark code is public but the table names no compiler version, flags, or which CPU produced each v1.5.x row, so first-party tier C.

corrections.caveats: Own-benchmark numbers on a tiny, cache-resident array (tools/simd_verification.cpp: TEST_SIZE 1024 doubles, one warm-up call, then the mean of TEST_ITERATIONS = 5 timed calls) with no compiler version or flags, so tier C. The v1.5.x table is labelled by the doc as historical and does not say which machine produced which row. The accuracy gap weakens the comparison: simd_verification accepts cos to 1e-9 (7-term polynomial, max error about 1e-10), so a 4.9x cos result is not like for like with libm. The libm baseline is whatever the build platform ships (MSVC UCRT, Apple libm, glibc), and glibc was not named. The corvus comparison is not independent: corvus is the same owner's (OldCrow) other project, issue #43 was opened and closed by that owner, and it compares libstats v2.4.1 against corvus v1.0.1; the owner declined to import the roughly 0.52 ULP libstats kernels into corvus because corvus exp and log keep correctly rounded (0-ULP) gates on NEON, and the issue closed on 2026-10-12 after corvus narrowed the gap (exp 2.4, log 3.9, erf 1.8, cos/sin 2.6 ns per element against libstats 1.0, 1.7, 1.4, 2.5). corvus's own PERFORMANCE document is the better reference for corvus vs libm. 1-star repository maintained by one author.

notes: Record checks out: primitive speedups, NEON exp 2.5-2.6x, and corvus issue #43 numbers all match their sources; methodology is a 1,024-element, 5-iteration mean in tools/simd_verification.cpp. Shortcomings: tiny cache-resident workload, no compiler/flags, unnamed libm, looser accuracy than libm for cos, and the corvus baseline is the same author's project (corvus is already listed in wave 13).

tier_reason: The README image img/exhaustive_search_sift1M.png is the paper's own table (citation markers, 'Section 3.2' footnote) and shows every claimed time against FAISS PQ ADC m x 8 and polysemous codes; the paper was published in IEEE TPAMI (May 2021, DOI 10.1109/TPAMI.2019.2952606, confirmed by search snippets only), so it is a peer-reviewed measurement; no CPU model, compiler or flags for the SIFT1M table, so not A. Upgraded from C on the peer-review evidence.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Numbers read from the README table image img/exhaustive_search_sift1M.png (query time per query in ms): 64-bit codes: FAISS PQ m x 8 5.50 ms (R@1 0.227, R@100 0.918); polysemous 1.19 ms (0.225 / 0.854); Quicker ADC m x {8,8} AVX512 BW 1.18 ms (0.223 / 0.918), i.e. about 4.7x faster than FAISS PQ at equal R@100 (derived from page data); m x {6,6,4} AVX512 BW 0.56 ms (0.179 / 0.859, about 9.8x faster at lower recall); m x {4,4} AVX512 BW 0.58 ms (0.158 / 0.807, about 9.5x). 128-bit codes: FAISS PQ 9.51 ms (0.446 / 0.998); polysemous 2.90 ms (0.447 / 0.987); Quicker ADC m x {8,8} AVX512 BW 2.36 ms (0.446 / 0.997, about 4.0x); m x {6,6,4} 0.99 ms (0.371 / 0.984, about 9.6x); m x {4,4} AVX512 BW 0.80 ms (0.313 / 0.964, about 11.9x). Against polysemous codes the margin is small: at 64 bits m x {8,8} ties polysemous on time (1.18 vs 1.19 ms) with higher R@100 (0.918 vs 0.854), and m x {6,6,4} is about 2.1x faster at equal R@100 (0.859 vs 0.854); at 128 bits m x {8,8} is about 1.2x faster (2.36 vs 2.90 ms) (all derived from page data). The non-exhaustive SIFT1000M and Deep1B figures are curves with no printed numbers.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 62 stars, 5 forks; fork of FAISS (179 commits); successor of the already-listed Quick ADC (technicolor-research/quick-adc)
corrections.caveats: Peer-reviewed (IEEE TPAMI, May 2021, DOI 10.1109/TPAMI.2019.2952606; arXiv 1812.09162), but the venue was confirmed only from search snippets because arXiv, doi.org, IEEE and EPFL Infoscience are blocked here; the README table comes from the technical report built on code commit d11c5af and the TPAMI text was not opened. No CPU model or compiler for the SIFT1M exhaustive table (the footnote says then-current processors lacked AVX512 VBMI, so a Skylake-SP class machine is implied; the SIFT1000M and Deep1B plots say only 'AWS m5 instances'). The FAISS baseline is the mid-2018 FAISS this fork branched from, and later FAISS releases added their own 4-bit fast-scan PQ path (not checked this session), so the baseline is dated. At equal recall (m x {8,8}) the gain over FAISS PQ is about 4x to 5x; the 10x figures are at lower recall, and against polysemous codes the gain is between a tie and about 2x. The 'Sequential' float rows in the same table (for example 25.8 ms for m x {4,4}) are the authors' own scalar versions, not a competitor. The m x {8} AVX512 VBMI row has no timing (hardware unavailable) and its 'up to 4 times' is a projection. Licence is mixed: Thomson Licensing's Quicker ADC changes are Clear BSD (not OSI-approved; explicitly no patent licence) on top of Facebook's BSD-3-Clause plus the inherited PATENTS file (Facebook Additional Grant of Patent Rights Version 2, which terminates on patent assertion against Facebook). Not a duplicate of Quick ADC: this repo is the later FAISS integration with AVX-512, irregular product quantizers and a separate paper. Abandoned since 2019-01-03.

notes: All table numbers verified from the README image; tier raised C to B on TPAMI publication (snippet-confirmed, paper text not opened). Shortcomings: dated mid-2018 FAISS baseline, 10x gains only at lower recall, small margin over polysemous codes, no CPU/compiler, Clear BSD core without patent grant, abandoned 2019. Related to the already-listed Quick ADC but a distinct project.

tier_reason: benchmark_url is null and the repository (README.txt plus SpacePruner/despacebenchmark.c) contains benchmark code against the scalar despace and Lemire's neontbl_despace but records no results anywhere; one search for the Lemire posts' mention of this work found nothing, so tier D.

corrections.workload: SpacePruner/despacebenchmark.c: remove whitespace (space, LF, CR; about 3% of bytes) from a 32 KiB random buffer refilled before each run, best of 100 runs, printed as nanoseconds per input byte under the label 'ns per operation' by an iOS app (gettimeofday timer with microsecond resolution); scalar despace, neontbl_despace (AArch64 only), neon_interleaved_despace and neon_unzipping_despace are timed; no results are recorded in the repo.
corrections.caveats: No measurements, so tier D, and the project is not widely referenced (11 stars); kept because it is the closest ARM relative of the already-listed Despacer (lemire/despacer). The code is a benchmark app only: results appear on-device when the user taps Run, and the timer is gettimeofday at microsecond resolution over a 32 KiB buffer, so per-byte figures would be coarse. The licence is the README.txt sentence 'This project and all of its code is public domain.' with no LICENSE file (no patent grant); the benchmark and scalar code are 'Originally written by Daniel Lemire', whose blog-code repository also states a public-domain intent, but copyright notices were removed from the copies (commit 'Added a README, and removed copyright notices.'). The 2017 Lemire blog posts that report NEON despacing timings were not opened (blogs blocked) and two WebSearch queries for them returned nothing usable. Abandoned since 2017-07-20.

notes: No numbers anywhere; confirmed at D and kept per the keep-and-document rule (not a reject). Shortcomings: no recorded results, iOS-only harness with a microsecond timer, README-only public-domain statement with no patent grant, abandoned 2017. Not a duplicate: it adds its own NEON kernels on top of Lemire's despacer code.
